questions.question: What is the difference between a physical and a paper trade?
questions.modelAnswer: A physical trade involves actual delivery of a commodity — real barrels loaded onto a vessel, real gas injected into a pipeline. A paper trade is a financial instrument (futures, swap, or option) that references a commodity price but typically doesn't result in delivery. Most traders use paper markets to hedge their physical exposure or take directional price views without managing logistics. The key distinction: physical trades require scheduling, shipping, and operational execution. Paper trades settle financially.
questions.framework: Follow up they might ask: 'Can a paper trade become physical?' Yes — if a futures contract is held to expiry without being closed, delivery can be required. This is rare but happens.
questions.interviewTip: Follow up they might ask: 'Can a paper trade become physical?' Yes — if a futures contract is held to expiry without being closed, delivery can be required. This is rare but happens.

questions.question: Explain contango and backwardation. Which is more common, and why?
questions.modelAnswer:
Contango is when forward prices are higher than spot prices — the curve slopes upward. It typically signals current oversupply or weak near-term demand. Storage costs, financing, and insurance (collectively 'cost of carry') set a floor for the contango level. If the contango is steeper than the cost of carry, traders will buy physical, store it, and sell forward — which arbitrages the curve back toward carry cost.

Backwardation is the inverse — spot prices exceed forward prices. It signals current tightness and rewards holders of physical commodity with positive roll yield.

Historically, oil markets spend more time in contango because producers hedge forward (selling futures to lock in prices), which pushes forward prices down relative to spot. Backwardation tends to be sharper but shorter-lived — it appears during genuine supply squeezes.
questions.framework: The depth of backwardation tells you how tight the physical market is. Very steep backwardation ('super-backwardation') often precedes a sharp correction once the squeeze resolves.
questions.interviewTip: The depth of backwardation tells you how tight the physical market is. Very steep backwardation ('super-backwardation') often precedes a sharp correction once the squeeze resolves.

questions.question: What is Dated Brent and why does it matter?
questions.modelAnswer:
Dated Brent is the benchmark price for physical North Sea crude oil, assessed daily by Platts (now S&P Global Commodity Insights) based on actual transactions in the Brent, Forties, Oseberg, Ekofisk, and Troll crude grades (BFOET). It is the most important oil price benchmark globally — the majority of internationally traded crude oil is priced as a differential to Dated Brent.

It matters because: (1) it reflects actual physical market transactions, not just futures; (2) long-term crude supply contracts reference it for price settlement; (3) the spread between Dated Brent and exchange-traded Brent futures (the EFP — Exchange for Physicals) is itself a closely watched indicator of physical market tightness.
questions.framework: Interviewers often follow up: 'What is the difference between Dated Brent and NYMEX WTI?' Dated Brent is a physical assessment for North Sea crude. NYMEX WTI is a US futures contract. They trade at a spread to each other (Brent-WTI spread) driven by US inventory levels, transportation costs, and quality differences.
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers often follow up: 'What is the difference between Dated Brent and NYMEX WTI?' Dated Brent is a physical assessment for North Sea crude. NYMEX WTI is a US futures contract. They trade at a spread to each other (Brent-WTI spread) driven by US inventory levels, transportation costs, and quality differences.

questions.question: What does FOB and DES mean in an LNG contract, and why does it matter commercially?
questions.modelAnswer:
FOB (Free on Board): the seller delivers LNG to the vessel at the export terminal. The buyer arranges and pays for shipping. Title transfers at the load port. The buyer has full commercial flexibility — they control vessel routing and can divert the cargo to wherever the price is highest.

DES (Delivered Ex-Ship): the seller arranges and pays for shipping and delivers LNG to the discharge terminal. Title transfers at the discharge port. The buyer has simpler logistics but less flexibility — they can't easily divert the cargo.

Commercially, FOB is more valuable for sophisticated buyers who want to trade around their cargoes. Most US LNG is sold FOB, which is why it became the marginal swing supply globally — buyers can direct it to Asia or Europe depending on price signals.
questions.framework: A strong candidate notes that destination flexibility clauses in the contract are separable from FOB/DES terms. A DES contract can still include destination flexibility, though this is less common.
questions.interviewTip: A strong candidate notes that destination flexibility clauses in the contract are separable from FOB/DES terms. A DES contract can still include destination flexibility, though this is less common.

questions.question: What is demurrage and who is responsible for it?
questions.modelAnswer:
Demurrage is a penalty charge paid to the shipowner when a vessel is detained at a port beyond the contractually agreed loading or discharge time (laytime). It compensates the shipowner for lost vessel earnings during the delay.

Who pays depends on why the delay occurred. If the cargo owner's terminal is congested, or their documentation was late, they pay demurrage. If the delay was caused by the shipowner's vessel having a mechanical fault, the charterer would dispute the demurrage claim. Charterparty terms define exactly what events start and stop the laytime clock — weather, waiting for berth, notice of readiness tendering times.
questions.framework: Demurrage is one of the most common sources of commercial disputes in physical trading. In interviews, showing you understand laytime calculation methodology and the NOR (Notice of Readiness) process signals real operational exposure.
questions.interviewTip: Demurrage is one of the most common sources of commercial disputes in physical trading. In interviews, showing you understand laytime calculation methodology and the NOR (Notice of Readiness) process signals real operational exposure.

questions.question: What is mark-to-market (MTM) and why is it important?
questions.modelAnswer:
Mark-to-market is the daily revaluation of open positions at current market prices. It converts unrealised gains and losses into a daily P&L figure. Every commodity desk does this at close of business each day.

It matters for three reasons: (1) it determines the unrealised P&L that management reviews daily; (2) for exchange-traded positions, it triggers margin calls if positions lose value — the firm must post additional collateral; (3) it provides the 'true' economic position of the desk, which may differ from the cash P&L until trades settle.

A common misunderstanding from finance candidates: in banking, many instruments are marked quarterly or held at cost. In commodity trading, everything is marked daily. A trader who can't explain their MTM move that day is considered not on top of their book.

questions.question: What is a crack spread?
questions.modelAnswer:
A crack spread is the price difference between crude oil (input) and the refined products derived from it (output). It represents the gross refinery margin — how much money a refinery makes per barrel of crude it processes before operating costs.

The most commonly cited is the 3-2-1 crack spread: 3 barrels of crude refined into 2 barrels of gasoline and 1 barrel of heating oil/diesel. The value of the products minus the cost of the crude is the crack.

Why it matters: crack spreads drive refinery run rates. Wide cracks = refiners run harder, buy more crude. Collapsed cracks = refiners cut throughput. Crude oil traders watch crack spreads closely because they directly drive physical crude demand.
questions.framework: Know at least one current rough number. 'I've been tracking the NWE hydrocracking margin which has been around $X/bbl recently because of strong diesel demand and limited new refinery capacity' shows genuine market awareness.
questions.interviewTip: Know at least one current rough number. 'I've been tracking the NWE hydrocracking margin which has been around $X/bbl recently because of strong diesel demand and limited new refinery capacity' shows genuine market awareness.

questions.question: What is VaR?
questions.modelAnswer:
Value at Risk (VaR) is a statistical measure of the maximum expected loss over a specified time period at a given confidence level. A VaR of $5M at 95% confidence over one day means there is a 5% probability of losing more than $5M in a single day.

In commodity trading, VaR is the primary metric used to set and monitor position limits. Each desk has a VaR limit; breaching it requires either reducing positions or getting explicit approval from senior risk management.

Important caveat: VaR tells you the loss you won't exceed 95% of the time — but it says nothing about the severity of losses in the remaining 5%. Tail risk, stress testing, and scenario analysis complement VaR precisely because of this limitation.
questions.framework: Strong candidates note the limitation without being asked: 'VaR is useful for normal market conditions but understates risk during tail events. That's why stress testing for supply disruption scenarios matters in commodity markets specifically.'
